prompt:
You read a student's answer to a question about a short Java program and decide which rules the answer engages with.

Program:
% java RandomSeq 5 > data.txt
% java Average < data.txt
% java RandomSeq 5 | java Average
(RandomSeq N prints N random numbers; Average reads numbers from standard input and prints their average)

Question: What appears in the terminal after each command? What does args[] contain when Average runs?

Student's answer: "1: nothing, the numbers go into data.txt. 2: the average. 3: an average of 5 new numbers, no file. args is empty."

Concept under consideration: redirection

Candidate edges of this concept. A misconception/error edge shows the wrong rule (logic) and the right rule (twin_logic); a concept edge shows the rule that links the two concepts; a level way (lvl:) shows one way an answer can display a level of understanding of the concept.
- lvl:redirection@L0#0 | level L0 way everyday_reading: In maths `<` and `>` mean less-than and greater-than. In a command line they are directives to the operating system: `< file` makes the file the standard input and `> file` sends standard output to the file. They are not part of Java or of args[].
- lvl:redirection@L0#2 | level L0 way inconsistent_trace: Points to LT (the OS connects the file before the program runs; reads come from the file and writes go only to the file). An uneven trace shows output on the screen as well as in the file, or treats the file name as a command-line argument. (here mixing in: "a redirected file shows up in args[]")
- lvl:redirection@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: Redirection is an operating-system (shell) mechanism that connects a program's standard input or standard output to a file.
- lvl:redirection@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: `java P > data.txt` writes standard output to data.txt instead of the terminal. `java P < data.txt` makes StdIn read from data.txt. The program itself is not changed.
- lvl:redirection@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: The shell opens the file and connects it before main starts. Each StdIn read then takes the next value from the file, and each print appends text at the end of the output file.
- lvl:redirection@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: `java RandomSeq 1000 > data.txt` prints nothing in the terminal and leaves a file of 1,000 values. `java Average < data.txt` prints their average.
- lvl:redirection@L2#2 | level L2 way one_step_execution: Each read or print still does exactly what it does at a terminal; only the source or destination is a file (one print appends to the file).
- lvl:redirection@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: `> file` diverts all standard output (print, println, printf) into the file, so nothing appears in the terminal.
- lvl:redirection@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: `< file` makes the file's contents the standard input stream: the same StdIn calls read the file's tokens in order.
- lvl:redirection@L3#2 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: `A > f` followed by `B < f` has the same effect as `A | B`, except that the pipe creates no file.
- lvl:redirection@L3#3 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: Redirecting different files into the same program changes the data it processes without changing the program.
- lvl:redirection@L3#4 | level L3 way purpose_of_the_whole: Redirection saves output for later and feeds large amounts of data from files, without typing.
- lvl:redirection@L4#0 | level L4 way predict_a_change: The program is unchanged whether its input or output is the terminal or a file: the I/O abstraction is conserved. Changing only the file changes only the data.
- lvl:redirection@L4#1 | level L4 way transfer_to_a_new_program: Use redirection when the data are in a file or the results should be saved. When a program needs several input or output files at once, use In/Out instead (one standard stream each way).
- lvl:redirection@L4#2 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: `> file` replaces the file's previous contents. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Redirecting output onto an existing data file (or onto the input file itself) overwrites it.
- lvl:redirection@L4#3 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: The input file must exist and be readable. Kind: launch error. Trigger class: `java Average < missing.txt`: the shell reports that the file does not exist, and the program never starts.
- lvl:redirection@L4#4 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: A redirected file is finite. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: The program reads more values than the file contains.
